definition: Roof replacement after a leak strips a roof whose chronic or widespread leaking has saturated the underlayment and deck, replaces rotted sheathing, and installs a new roof system. It applies when a leak recurs across repairs or has rotted the deck so that a surface repair cannot reverse the moisture damage. It addresses systemic failure rather than the isolated detail a single repair would patch.

signs: **Three or more roof repairs in 2 years** signal a systemic failure rather than an isolated leak, the contractor-consensus 3-repairs rule that favors replacement, per WeatherShield repair-vs-replace guidance.

**A leak path across more than 25-30% of the roof area** crosses the contractor-consensus 25% rule, the threshold above which full replacement costs less than continued spot repair, per roofing industry guidance.
**A repair quote approaching 50% of replacement cost** crosses the contractor-consensus 50% rule, the point at which replacement returns more value than another repair, per roofing industry guidance.

**Daylight visible through the roof deck from inside the attic** indicates holes in the decking and shingles, a direct breach that points toward replacement rather than a patch, per InterNACHI and This Old House inspection guidance.

**Soft, spongy, or crumbling sheathing, delaminated plywood, or swollen OSB edges** indicate a moisture-rotted deck from a prolonged leak, because saturated sheathing loses the ability to grip a roofing nail, per InterNACHI.
**A sagging ceiling or roofline** indicates sheathing decay from prolonged moisture and ranks as a structural priority, per GAF inspection guidance.

**Brown or yellow ceiling stains that return after each rainfall** indicate an active recurring leak, because a recurring stain marks ongoing moisture intrusion rather than a one-time event, per GAF and This Old House inspection guidance.

**Recurring leaks in the same spot on a low-slope roof** indicate a systemic membrane failure regardless of the damaged percentage, the point a flat roof replaces rather than patches, per HomeAdvisor flat-roof guidance.

**Roughly 90-95% of roof leaks originate at flashing details** and only 5-10% at the open shingle field, so flashing leaks that recur across the roof point to systemic failure, an industry estimate attributed to the NRCA.
selectionCriteria: Confirm the contractor holds active New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor registration under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136, with the 13VH registration number shown on the contract and advertising per N.J.S.A. 56:8-144 — this is a registration, not a roofing license, because New Jersey issues no roofing license.
Verify at least $500,000 per occurrence in commercial general liability coverage under N.J.S.A. 56:8-142 by requesting a certificate of insurance directly from the carrier.
Require a written contract for any project over $500 per N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2, with an itemized written estimate setting scope, labor, materials, and timeline before work begins.

Require a documented leak assessment that traces the recurring leak to its root-cause detail and applies the 3-repairs, 25%, and 50% repair-vs-replace thresholds before a replacement is quoted, per WeatherShield and roofing industry guidance.

Confirm the contractor will strip the leaked roof to the bare deck and replace rotted sheathing rather than recover over it, because IRC Section R908 prohibits a new covering over a water-soaked or deteriorated deck and N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 requires complete removal of a water-soaked covering.

Ask for local Essex County references and confirm the contractor issues a written workmanship warranty on the labor, separate from the manufacturer material warranty preserved by installing to manufacturer specification, per Owens Corning warranty guidance.

On a storm-driven or insurance leak claim, confirm the contractor documents the damage with timestamped photographs and meets the adjuster on site but does not negotiate or settle the claim — under N.J.S.A. 17:22B only the homeowner or a licensed public adjuster may negotiate the claim, and no contractor may waive the deductible, promise a free roof, or guarantee approval.

technicalFacts.fact: The 3-repairs rule favors replacement after 3 or more repairs in 2 years, the 25% rule after damage crosses 25-30% of the roof area, and the 50% rule when one repair approaches 50% of replacement cost.
technicalFacts.source: WeatherShield and roofing industry repair-vs-replace guidance (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: A localized repair costs 5 to 10 times less than replacement only while the roof stays under 10 to 15 years old and the damage stays localized.
technicalFacts.source: Home Depot and Kelly Roofing cost data (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: Trapped moisture from a prolonged leak decays sheathing until it loses the ability to grip a roofing nail, and roofing nails penetrate at least three-quarters of an inch into solid deck, so deteriorated plywood or OSB is replaced rather than roofed over.
IRC Section R908 prohibits installing a new covering over a water-soaked or deteriorated deck, and the NJ Rehabilitation Subcode requires complete removal of a water-soaked covering.
technicalFacts.source: ICC IRC Section R908 and N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 (per gold and fact pack)

technicalFacts.fact: The IRC ice-barrier provision requires a self-adhering ice barrier, or two cemented underlayment layers, from the eave to a point at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line; ice-and-water shield self-seals around fasteners.
technicalFacts.source: ICC IRC Section R905.1.2 and ASTM D1970 (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: Installing the cover to manufacturer specification preserves the material warranty that covers factory defects, which is separate from the written workmanship warranty that backs the labor.

Roof-covering lifespans against which a leaked roof is judged: 3-tab asphalt about 20 years, architectural asphalt about 30 years, metal 40 to 80 years, slate 60 to 150 years; on low-slope roofs EPDM 15 to 25 years, TPO 7 to 20 years, modified bitumen about 20 years.
A low-slope roof needs at least one-quarter inch per foot of slope to drain, and ponding water remaining more than 48 hours counts as a defect that breaks down membrane seams.

A complete tear-off and replacement of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling counts as ordinary maintenance and requires no construction permit, while a structural change to rotted rafters or trusses still triggers a permit; on a commercial building a roof replacement requires a permit because the ordinary-maintenance exemption covers only repair of up to 25% of the total roof area in a 12-month period.
technicalFacts.source: N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7, NJ Uniform Construction Code (per gold)

technicalFacts.fact: Homeowners insurance covers roof replacement when a covered peril causes the damage (wind, hail, a falling tree, or fire) and excludes replacement for normal wear, age, or deferred maintenance, so a long-neglected chronic leak often falls outside coverage; wind and hail rank as the largest claim type at 2.8% of insured homes per year (1 in 36), with an average claim near $14,747.

In New Jersey only a licensed public adjuster or an attorney may negotiate or settle a first-party property-insurance claim on behalf of the insured; a roofing contractor may inspect, photograph and document the damage, write a scope and estimate, and meet the adjuster on site, but may not negotiate the claim, waive or pay the deductible, promise a free roof, or guarantee approval.
technicalFacts.source: N.J.S.A. 17:22B (Public Adjusters' Licensing Act); NJ DOBI (per fact pack)

defabToKill.issue: "Mold growth behind walls and insulation develops within 48 hours of sustained moisture." — unsourced mold-timeline claim not in the gold.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the mold-timeline assertion. Ground hidden-damage signs in the gold/InterNACHI deck-rot facts: a prolonged leak rots sheathing until it loses the ability to grip a roofing nail (soft/spongy/delaminated deck), per InterNACHI; replacement with full deck exposure reveals deterioration a patch cannot.

defabToKill.issue: "a condition common in homes roofed before NJ adopted the 2009 IRC requirement for ice barrier installation" and "common in Montclair and South Orange," "endemic in Essex County's piecemeal addition culture" — invented local/historical specifics and a wrong code-adoption year not in the gold or fact pack.
defabToKill.fix: Replace with the gold's sourced ice-barrier provision (IRC Section R905.1.2 requires the ice barrier from the eave to at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line, per ASTM D1970 self-sealing) and the NRCA flashing-origin estimate (90-95% of leaks originate at flashing). Drop the city-name color and the unsourced '2009 IRC' adoption date.

defabToKill.issue: "In Essex County's older homes, systemic leaks often indicate..." and "decades of slow leaks create conditions where the roof deck is structurally compromised across large areas" — qualitative narrative without the gold's sourced thresholds.
defabToKill.fix: Anchor the single-point-vs-systemic distinction to the gold's contractor-consensus rules: 3 or more repairs in 2 years (WeatherShield), damage across 25-30% of the roof, a repair near 50% of replacement cost, and recurring same-spot low-slope leaks (HomeAdvisor) — each a named-source replacement signal.

defabToKill.issue: "$8,500-$15,000 for asphalt shingles on a typical Essex County home" and "leak-driven replacements average 15-25% higher" — invented flat total and an invented 15-25% premium, both unsourced and conflicting with the gold.
defabToKill.fix: Use the gold's sourced figures: a NJ roof replacement runs $10,000-$25,000 for a typical home (HomeAdvisor, Modernize), with NJ architectural asphalt at $6.50-$11.00/sq ft (Josten Roofing). State that a leaked roof adds re-decking cost rather than a fabricated percentage premium.

defabToKill.issue: "Deck repair averages $300-$800 per sheet of plywood replacement. A chronic leak that has been running for months may require 4-8 sheets, adding $1,200-$6,400 to the project." — invented per-sheet and aggregate figures not in the gold.
defabToKill.fix: Replace with the gold's sourced re-decking figure: re-decking runs $2 to $5 per square foot, per HomeGuide, and N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 requires full removal of a water-soaked covering. Do not state per-sheet dollar amounts or a sheet count.

defabToKill.issue: "balloon-frame construction common in pre-1950 neighborhoods," plus the interior-restoration price list: "ceiling drywall replacement ($200-$600 per area), painting ($300-$800 per room), insulation replacement... ($1-$3 per square foot), and mold remediation if detected ($500-$5,000...)" — invented dollar figures and trades NQR does not perform.
defabToKill.fix: Cut the invented interior price list and the balloon-frame narrative. Keep cost scope to the roof: replacement total ($10,000-$25,000), per-sf material (Josten), and re-decking ($2-$5/sq ft, HomeGuide). NQR is a roofing contractor; do not quote drywall/paint/mold prices.

defabToKill.issue: "NJ requires licensed mold remediation for areas exceeding 25 square feet." — an unsourced regulatory claim; NJ has no such statute named in the fact pack, and mold remediation is outside NQR's scope.
defabToKill.fix: Remove the mold-remediation regulatory claim. NQR is a registered NJ HIC roofing contractor, not licensed to remediate mold; do not assert a NJ mold-area threshold that no named source supports.

defabToKill.issue: "Standard NJ homeowners insurance covers sudden and accidental water damage but excludes gradual leaks from maintenance neglect... a roof that leaked during a specific storm event qualifies for coverage" and "contractors experienced in insurance work can help establish the causation link" — overstated coverage certainty and an implied claims-assistance role.
defabToKill.fix: Use the gold's compliant framing: homeowners insurance covers replacement when a covered peril (wind, hail, falling tree, fire) causes the damage and excludes normal wear, age, or deferred maintenance, so a long-neglected chronic leak often falls outside coverage (Insurance Information Institute). NQR documents the damage with timestamped photographs for the adjuster; under N.J.S.A. 17:22B only the homeowner or a licensed public adjuster negotiates the claim.

defabToKill.issue: "Professional temporary repairs cost $200-$800 and protect your home reliably for weeks or months." — invented temporary-repair price range not in the gold.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the dollar range. Describe temporary stabilization (tarping to stop further interior water entry) qualitatively as a stabilization-first step, then the repair-vs-replace assessment, without a fabricated price.

defabToKill.issue: "Essex County's humidity levels mean... Industrial fans and dehumidifiers may be needed for 2-5 days after deck exposure to reach acceptable moisture content." and "Moisture meters and infrared scanning" — invented drying-time figures and equipment specifics not in the gold.
defabToKill.fix: Replace with the gold-grounded code rule: a new covering cannot be installed over a water-soaked or deteriorated deck (IRC Section R908; N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 requires complete removal of a water-soaked covering), so the rotted sheathing is stripped to bare deck and replaced rather than dried-in-place. Drop the 2-5 day drying figure.

defabToKill.issue: "our crews install ice-and-water shield up to six feet from eave lines (double the code minimum) and run full-width membrane through all valleys. These upgrades add minimal cost..." — a 'six feet / double the code minimum' claim that misstates the actual code provision and an unsourced cost characterization.
defabToKill.fix: State the real provision: IRC Section R905.1.2 requires the ice barrier from the eave to a point at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line (ASTM D1970 self-sealing around fasteners). Frame enhanced detailing at former leak points qualitatively; do not invent a 'six feet, double the minimum' figure or a cost claim.

defabToKill.issue: "Mold growth behind walls and insulation" / moisture-remediation framing positions NQR doing remediation; and "Bucket-and-towel management is not acceptable" — casual tone and out-of-scope remediation.
defabToKill.fix: Keep the decision overview within roofing scope and answer-first: the defining factor is the repair-vs-replace threshold plus the code bar on recovering a water-soaked deck. NQR stabilizes, assesses against the 3-repairs/25%/50% rules, tears off to bare deck, replaces rotted sheathing, and installs ice barrier + underlayment + cover to manufacturer spec. Remove casual phrasing and remediation claims.

parentDebtToAvoid: Do NOT reproduce the gold's commercial brand-roster line 'Newark Quality Roofing installs and services Firestone, Carlisle, and Johns Manville membrane systems.' — name membrane types (EPDM, TPO, modified bitumen) generically, not NQR-branded partnerships.

Do NOT reproduce the gold credentialsHighlight chip 'NJ HIC Licensed' — NQR is a registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor (registration under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136), NOT licensed; NJ issues no roofing license. Use 'registered NJ HIC' / 'registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor'.

Do NOT frame GAF/Owens Corning/InterNACHI/NRCA as NQR certifications or partnerships (no Master Elite, SELECT ShingleMaster, Preferred, Golden Pledge, or '~2% qualify'); name them only as external data, warranty, or inspection-guidance sources.

Do NOT carry any 'licensed' framing for NQR's own credential anywhere (whyChooseUs, FAQs, body); reframe to 'registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor' and keep liability coverage tied to the Contractors Registration Act / N.J.S.A. 56:8-142.
Do NOT invent NQR project counts ('hundreds of roofs/replacements'); NQR is a registered NJ HIC serving Essex County with no stated counts.

On any insurance/storm angle do NOT imply NQR negotiates, files, manages, maximizes, or guarantees the claim, waives/covers the deductible, or promises a free roof — enforce the N.J.S.A. 17:22B hard line (document + meet adjuster on site only).

articleAngles.signs: Definitively state the named-source thresholds that turn a leak into a replacement: 3 or more repairs in 2 years (WeatherShield), a leak path across 25-30% of the roof, a repair near 50% of replacement cost, daylight or soft/spongy/delaminated deck from a chronic leak (InterNACHI), and recurring same-spot low-slope membrane leaks (HomeAdvisor). The lead answer (<=40w) names the controlling signal: a leak that recurs across repairs or has rotted the deck calls for replacement, not another patch.
articleAngles.costGuide: There IS a real whole-job total for this service: a NJ roof replacement runs $10,000-$25,000 for a typical home (HomeAdvisor, Modernize), with NJ architectural asphalt at $6.50-$11.00/sq ft (Josten Roofing) and rotted-deck re-decking adding $2-$5/sq ft (HomeGuide); labor is roughly 60-70% of the total. The directAnswer leads with that $10,000-$25,000 total, then notes a leaked roof adds re-decking cost because N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 requires removing a water-soaked covering.
articleAngles.decision: The single thing a homeowner must understand: a roof leaked long enough to rot the deck cannot be recovered or patched back to health — IRC Section R908 and N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 prohibit installing a new covering over a water-soaked or deteriorated deck, so the defining decision is repair-vs-replace judged against the 3-repairs / 25% / 50% thresholds, after which a full tear-off to bare deck (replacing rotted sheathing) is the only code-compliant fix. The lead answer states that a chronic-leak replacement ends a recurring leak by resetting the whole underlayment-and-cover system rather than patching the detail that admits water.
